narratives.narrative: The characteristic here is 'rage' typed as an affect (D102 type=affect) — not yet a plan but the raw heat of revolt. Its sense (D101) is 'nations rage': the massed peoples seethe. The bearer (D105) is the nations themselves; the operation (D106) is a collective seething in tumultuous uproar against the LORD and his anointed — fury as a corporate interior state. The target (D107) registers as 'tumult', i.e. the fury pours out into uproar rather than toward a discrete object it means to change, and the coupling (D112) binds the state to 'rage' itself. Crucially the locus (D116) is internal:ib-state — an interior condition of the peoples — and the role (D115) is a genuine characteristic, not a mere qualifier. The discovery note (D114) reads v1 as the churning uproar of the massed peoples, emotion before scheme. Now the silences, which are evidence. No source (D103 present:false) — the text does not say what kindles the rage; it is presented as arising, uncaused, from within the collective. No seat (D104=none) — the fury is not lodged in a named organ (heart, bowels); it is diffuse, a whole-body corporate heat, not organ-located. No manner (D108=none), no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent): the rage is given bare, without described texture or measured degree. No effect (D111 absent) — the verse holds the emotion at its boiling point, before consequence. No prohibition (D113 absent) — it is described, not forbidden. In the inner-being frame God and his anointed are the arena the fury is directed against, but the reading stays on the human interior — a shared, sourceless, seatless, boundless heat of rebellion.
narratives.story: In the opening of this psalm whole nations are pictured boiling over with fury against God and his chosen king. It is not yet a scheme, just raw heat — a crowd seething with rage. The poem never says what set them off; the anger simply rises from inside them, as if from nowhere. It is not pinned to any one part of a person, nor given any particular shape or measured strength — it is simply a shared, churning uproar. And the verse leaves it there, at full boil, without yet telling us what it leads to. What we see is a whole people's inner life burning with revolt, with God as the one it burns against.

narratives.narrative: Here anger is typed not as an affect that simply happens but as volition (D102 type=volition) — something the hearer is summoned to govern. The sense (D101) is the command 'be angry and do not sin.' The bearer (D105) is the hearer addressed; the operation (D106) is anger permitted yet fenced: the passion is neither denied nor indulged but disciplined — felt without being let spill into sin. Tellingly the target (D107) is 'disciplined-anger' itself — the object of the work is the emotion, turned back on itself to be mastered; the coupling (D112) binds 'angry' to 'not-sin', the two held in a single tether. The locus (D116) is internal:ib-state and the role (D115) a characteristic: a real interior movement, not a label. The discovery (D114) names it the governing of a strong emotion — restraint short of wrongdoing, not suppression. The silences sharpen this. No source (D103 present:false) — the provocation is not named, because the point is not what stirs the anger but what one does with it. No seat (D104=none) — not lodged in a bodily organ (the next clause moves to 'ponder in your hearts', but the anger itself is not seated). No manner (D108=none), no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent): the anger is given without texture or degree, because the command concerns its boundary, not its heat. No effect (D111 absent): the outcome is left open — the verse legislates the handling, not the result. Strikingly, no prohibition on the anger itself (D113 absent) — anger is not forbidden; only its spilling into sin is fenced. Within the inner-being frame this is the rare disciplined pole of the family: the human interior told it may burn, but under restraint.
narratives.story: This verse does something surprising with anger — it does not condemn it. It tells the listener: go ahead and be angry, but do not let it tip over into wrongdoing. The work here is self-mastery: to feel the heat and hold it, neither smothering it nor letting it run wild. The poem never says what provoked the anger, because that is not the point; it never locates the feeling in one part of a person or measures how fierce it is. What matters is the fence around it. And notice — the anger itself is never called sin; only letting it break loose is. It is a picture of a person governing a strong emotion from within.

narratives.narrative: 'Fret' enters the family as volition (D102 type=volition), a movement the hearer is charged to refuse. Its sense (D101) is the double command 'fret not, be not envious of evildoers.' The bearer (D105) is the hearer; the operation (D106) is the self told not to burn over the wicked — refusing the corrosive envy stirred by their prosperity. The target (D107) is 'refusing-envy' — again the object is the inner heat itself, to be quelled; the coupling (D112) ties the state to its own negation, 'fret-not'. Locus (D116) internal:ib-state, role (D115) characteristic. The discovery (D114) reads it as the disciplining of a specific inner unrest: the interior refuses to burn with envy at the wicked's success. This is anger's near-neighbour — resentful agitation — met here by prohibition-in-the-form-of-command. The silences: no source named (D103 present:false), though the surrounding passage supplies the occasion (the evildoers' prosperity); the row itself leaves the origin unstated. No seat (D104=none) — not organ-lodged. No manner (D108=none), no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent): the fret is given bare, its boundary rather than its texture in view. No effect (D111 absent) — though the wider psalm warns fretting 'tends only to evil' (v8), this anchor row records no traced outcome. No prohibition row (D113 absent) even though the sense is itself a prohibition — the forbidding is carried inside the operation, not flagged separately. In the inner-being frame the wicked are the occasion in the arena, but the reading holds on the hearer's interior, called to refuse a smouldering, envious agitation.
narratives.story: This psalm opens with a warning against a very ordinary temptation: stewing over people who do wrong and seem to get away with it. Do not fret, it says, and do not envy them. The task is inward — to refuse the slow burn of resentment that the success of the wicked stirs up. The poem does not spell out exactly what sparks the feeling, or where in a person it sits, or how hot it gets; it simply calls the person to put it out. It is anger's quieter cousin, a gnawing agitation, and here the command is plain: don't let it take hold.

narratives.narrative: Here anger (Hebrew aph) is typed as a status (D102 type=status) — not an act but a settled condition. Its sense (D101): 'in anger they bear a grudge.' The bearer (D105) is the enemies; the target (D107) is the psalmist, against whom the anger is held. Notably the operation (D106=none): this is the striking silence — the anger here does nothing, performs no verb; it is a state resting in the enemies rather than a movement breaking out. That absence is the finding: aph has settled, hardened from a flaring into a fixed hostility. The coupling (D112) is an explicit span-pair — anger bound to 'the grudge they cherish' — so the reading is anger fused to a nursed resentment. Locus (D116) internal:ib-state; role (D115) characteristic. The discovery (D114) names it the enemies' hot hostility, aph as the burning resentment out of which they cherish enmity — anger settled into grudge. The other silences: no source (D103 present:false) — what first kindled it is unstated; it is simply borne. No seat (D104=none) — not organ-lodged, though aph literally evokes the flaring nostril, the row records no bodily seat. No manner (D108=none), no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent), no effect (D111 absent), no prohibition (D113 absent): the anger is given as a bare, settled, targeted state without described texture, degree, or traced consequence. In the inner-being frame the psalmist is the object in the arena, but the reading is on the enemies' interior — a hot resentment that has cooled into a permanent grudge.
narratives.story: In this lament the poet's enemies are described as holding a grudge against him 'in anger.' What is striking is that the anger here does not do anything — it doesn't strike or shout; it simply sits in them as a settled hostility. It has cooled from a flare-up into a fixed, nursed resentment, tied directly to the grudge they keep against him. The poem never says what first set it off, or where it lives inside them, or how fiercely it burns; it just names it as a hot dislike that has hardened into something permanent, aimed squarely at him.
narratives.variation_note: One of two readings of aph (H0639:anger). At Psa 55:3 aph is a status with operation:none — anger frozen into a borne grudge against the psalmist; at Psa 124:3 the same word is a state whose operation is 'have anger ignite', fury flaring to swallow its victim alive. The difference is state-vs-event and settled-vs-kindling: here anger is a cold, nursed condition; there it is a hot, igniting motion. Same word, opposite temperature of movement — evidence that aph spans both the smouldering grudge and the sudden blaze.

narratives.narrative: chemah — literally heat/venom/wrath — is read here as a status (D102 type=status), a poisonous condition the wicked possess rather than an act they perform. The sense (D101) is 'venom / poison-wrath': they have venom. The bearer (D105) is the wicked. As at Psa 55, both operation (D106=none) and target (D107=none) are absent, and that double silence is the point: this venom is not shown striking anyone in particular — it is a constitutional toxicity, malice held in the inner being as a property, not yet a deed. What the row does carry is manner (D108): 'like the venom of a serpent, a deaf adder' — the one described texture, a simile of reptilian poison. The coupling (D112) is an explicit span-pair linking the venom to the wilful refusal to hear (v5): the malice is welded to incorrigibility — a deaf adder that will not be charmed. The discovery (D114) makes this explicit: malice as deadly poison, worse for being uncharmable — venom joined to stubborn deafness. Locus (D116) internal:ib-state; role (D115) characteristic. Remaining silences: no source (D103 present:false) — the venom is innate, un-originated in the text (v3 says estranged 'from the womb'); no seat (D104=none) — not organ-lodged despite chemah's heat-imagery; no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent), no effect (D111 absent) — the poison's outworking is not traced here; no prohibition (D113 absent). In the inner-being frame there is no human victim named as target — the reading rests wholly on the wicked's interior: a settled, serpent-like, un-charmable poison of the soul.
narratives.story: Here the wicked are said to carry venom inside them, like the poison of a snake. The picture is not of them biting someone in this moment, but of poison simply being in them — malice as part of who they are. And it is worse than a snake's, the poem adds: they are like a deaf adder that refuses to hear the snake-charmer, so the venom can never be coaxed out or calmed. Where this hatred came from is not said — it is treated as inborn — and it is not pinned to any one place in them, or shown doing its damage yet. What we are left with is a portrait of an inner life that is toxic and stubbornly closed, poison that will not be charmed away.

narratives.narrative: 'Fierce men' (Hebrew az, strong/fierce) is typed as a status (D102 type=status) — a quality of the enemies rather than a discrete act. The sense (D101): fierce, strong men who stir up strife. The bearer (D105) is the fierce enemies. Here the silences pile up: operation (D106=none), target (D107=none), and manner (D108=none) — three empty dimensions. This is the thinnest reading: the fierceness is asserted as a trait, but the row records no operation it performs, no object it strikes, no described manner. What anchors it is the coupling (D112), an explicit span-pair binding the fierce men to 'their stirring up strife' — their fierceness is known by the discord they raise. The discovery (D114) fills this out: mighty, ruthless foes who band against the psalmist though he has done no wrong (v3-4) — fierceness as unprovoked aggression. Most distinctive is the locus (D116): external:person — alone in this family, this reading is placed outside the inner-being interior, on the persons of the enemies rather than as an inner state. That single flag is a real finding: 'fierce men' reads less as an interior emotion than as a description of hostile agents, hovering at the family's edge (its cluster is 'Strength', not Anger). Remaining silences: no source (D103 present:false) — their fierceness is not accounted for; no seat (D104=none); no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent), no effect (D111 absent), no prohibition (D113 absent). In the inner-being frame this is the boundary case — the arena's aggressors named as such, their interior barely opened, their fierceness read as the outward strength of hostile men.
narratives.story: In this cry for rescue the poet is surrounded by fierce, powerful men who stir up trouble against him — and, he insists, he has done nothing to deserve it. The poem calls them fierce almost as a plain fact about who they are, rather than describing a particular thing they feel or do; it does not say what drives them, or trace their fierceness to any inner spark, or measure it. Really this is a description of dangerous people more than of a feeling inside them — the odd one out in this group, pointing outward at the enemies themselves. What holds it together is the strife they raise: you know their fierceness by the conflict they create around an innocent man.

narratives.narrative: chemah appears again, now typed as a state (D102 type=state), 'the wrath of man.' The bearer (D105) is man / humanity — this is human fury in general. What sets this reading apart is the operation (D106), the one anchor where wrath's motion is not 'none' but a span-linked event: 'turned to praise God.' The wrath does not reach its own intended object; instead it is redirected — its outworking is that even hostile rage is made to serve God's glory (manner, D108). The target (D107=none) is itself telling: the wrath's intended victim is not registered, because the point is that its trajectory is hijacked — it lands not where it aimed but on praise. The coupling (D112) is an explicit span-pair binding the wrath to 'the praise it is made to render.' The discovery (D114) draws it out: human fury, even in rebellion, God turns to his own honour; chemah overruled becomes an instrument of praise, with a residue God simply restrains (the 'remnant of wrath', v10b). Locus (D116) internal:ib-state; role (D115) characteristic. The silences: no source (D103 present:false) — what kindles man's wrath is unstated, taken as given; no seat (D104=none); no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent), no effect flagged separately (D111 absent) though the operation itself carries the outcome; no prohibition (D113 absent). In the inner-being frame God is the arena that overrules, but the reading holds on the human interior: wrath as a hot state whose native motion is thwarted and turned — the rare case where the family's dark heat is neither condemned nor indulged but conscripted, and its surplus leashed.
narratives.story: This verse makes a bold claim: even human rage ends up praising God. The furious anger of people, which means to do harm, is turned around so that it serves God's glory instead — it never quite reaches the target it aimed at, because it is redirected into praise. Whatever fury is left over that cannot be used this way, the poem says, God simply holds back, like a belt cinched tight. It does not explain what makes people rage, or where the anger sits, or how intense it is; the whole interest is in its being overruled. It is the one place here where this hot, dangerous feeling is neither forbidden nor let loose, but quietly put to work.

narratives.narrative: With tavah the family shifts from a felt state to an action (D102 type=action): to provoke, and specifically to pain or wound. The sense (D101) is 'provoke / pain.' The bearer (D105) is 'they' (Israel in the wilderness); the operation (D106) is to provoke / wound; the target (D107) is the Holy One of Israel. Unlike the settled-status readings, here the movement is fully traced: an agent performs an act of provocation upon an object. The coupling (D112) pairs it with 'the testing' — the provoking is bound up with their repeated testing of God (v41). The discovery (D114) reads it as the wounding of the Holy One by the limits they set on him. The locus (D116) is external:god — the movement is directed outward, at God, rather than resting as an inner state; this is provocation-as-deed, its centre of gravity in the arena. Role (D115) characteristic. The silences: no source (D103 present:false) — the inner spring of the provocation (unbelief, hardness) is not named in this row; no seat (D104=none) — not organ-lodged; no manner (D108=none) — the how of the provoking is unstated; no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent), no effect (D111 absent) — the outcome (God's restrained anger, v38) is not traced in this anchor; no prohibition (D113 absent). In the inner-being frame this is one of the 'provoke' cluster where the human interior is read chiefly through what it does to God: the inner being expressed as an act that wounds, its emotional root left implicit and its locus thrown outward onto its divine object.
narratives.story: Here the people are described as provoking God — actually wounding him — again and again in the wilderness. This is anger seen from the other side: not a feeling boiling up in them, but something they do to another, hurting the Holy One of Israel by the limits they keep placing on him. It goes hand in hand with their constant testing of him. The poem does not dwell on what was churning inside them, or where the impulse sat, or how it felt; it fixes on the act and its victim. It is the inner life shown through the damage it inflicts, aimed outward at God.

narratives.narrative: kaas here is an action (D102 type=action): 'provoke to anger.' The sense (D101) is the same. Bearer (D105) 'they'; operation (D106) to provoke to anger; target (D107) God. Like tavah in the prior passage, this is provocation-as-deed, the full agent-act-object motion traced. The coupling (D112) pairs it with 'moving him to jealousy by their idols' — the provoking is welded to their idolatry, which is its instrument. The discovery (D114) names it the deliberate rousing of God's anger by their idolatry — note 'deliberate': this is not accidental but a chosen provocation. Locus (D116) external:god — directed outward at God; role (D115) characteristic. The silences: no source (D103 present:false) — the interior root (their apostate hearts, v57) is not flagged in this row; no seat (D104=none); no manner (D108=none); no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent), no effect (D111 absent) — the consequence (God 'full of wrath', v59) is left untraced in the anchor row; no prohibition (D113 absent). In the inner-being frame the reading again reads the human interior through its outward act against God: an inner disposition expressed as the deliberate kindling of divine anger, its locus thrown onto God, its emotional interior implicit behind the deed of idolatry.
narratives.story: This verse pictures the people deliberately stirring up God's anger by building pagan shrines and worshipping idols. As with the wounding described earlier, the focus is not on a feeling rising inside them but on what they do to God — provoking him, making him jealous, on purpose. Their idol-worship is the very means by which they goad him. The poem does not describe the mood behind it, or where it sat in them, or how strong it was; it names the act and points it straight at God. This is the inner life read through a chosen provocation aimed outward.

narratives.narrative: kaas again as an action (D102 type=action), 'provoke.' Sense (D101) provoke. Bearer (D105) the fathers; operation (D106) provoke to anger; target (D107) the LORD, provoked 'by their deeds.' The full movement is traced: agent, act, divine object, and named instrument (their deeds — here the Baal of Peor, v28). The coupling (D112) is flagged 'external:god' — the provocation is coupled outward to God as the one roused. The discovery (D114) reads v29: they provoked the LORD to anger with their deeds, and the provocation is immediately met by plague. Distinctively, the locus row (D116) does not carry an inner/outer state-tag here but reads 'paired with the plague and Phinehas' intervention' — that is, this reading is anchored to its consequence: the provocation issues in plague, stayed only by Phinehas' intervention (v30). So where other rows leave effect untraced, here the outcome is folded into the locus flag — the deed and its judgement are bound together. Role (D115) characteristic. The silences: no source (D103 present:false) — the interior spring not named; no seat (D104=none); no manner (D108=none); no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent); no separate effect row (D111 absent) though the consequence surfaces in the locus flag; no prohibition (D113 absent). In the inner-being frame the human interior is again read through its outward act against God — provocation as deed — but uniquely tied here to the judgement it triggers, the plague that answers the rousing of divine anger.
narratives.story: At Peor the people provoke God to anger through their corrupt worship, and this time the poem ties the provocation straight to what follows: a deadly plague breaks out, halted only when Phinehas steps in. As with the other scenes of provoking, the interest is not in a feeling swelling inside them but in the act aimed at God and the judgement it brings down. Their deeds are the means by which they rouse him. The poem does not describe an inner mood, or where it sat, or how fierce it was; it binds the provocation to its terrible result. It is the inner life read through a deed that calls down disaster.

narratives.narrative: qatsaph enters as an action (D102 type=action), 'anger' in the sense of to provoke-to-wrath. Sense (D101) anger. Bearer (D105) the fathers; operation (D106) anger / provoke; target (D107) God, at the waters of Meribah. The motion is traced as agent-act-object. As at v29, the coupling (D112) is flagged 'external:god' — coupled outward to the God who is angered. The discovery (D114) reads v32: they angered him at Meribah, and its fallout reached even Moses. The locus row (D116) again carries not a state-tag but a consequence-pairing: 'paired with Moses' embittered spirit' — the provocation is bound to its collateral effect, the embittering of Moses' spirit so that 'he spoke rashly' (v33). So this reading, like its neighbour, folds the outcome into the locus: the people's provoking of God spills over to wound their mediator. Role (D115) characteristic. The silences: no source (D103 present:false); no seat (D104=none); no manner (D108=none); no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent); no separate effect (D111 absent) though the fallout appears in the locus flag; no prohibition (D113 absent). In the inner-being frame the human interior is read through its provoking act against God at Meribah — and distinctively through the ripple it sends into another human interior, Moses', which it embitters. The family's provocation here has a second victim: the mediator's own inner peace.
narratives.story: At the waters of Meribah the people anger God again — and the poem notes a sad side-effect: the trouble spilled over onto Moses, souring his spirit until he spoke rashly. Once more the focus is on the act of provoking God rather than on a feeling inside the people; this is the rousing of God's wrath by their rebellion. What makes this one distinct is the collateral damage: their provocation embittered their own leader. The poem does not describe the people's inner mood, or locate it, or measure it; it links their provoking to the wound it left in Moses. It is anger that harms not only its target but a bystander caught in its wake.

narratives.narrative: Here kaas is typed as a state (D102 type=state) rather than an action: 'the wicked man sees it and is angry.' Sense (D101) angry. Bearer (D105) the wicked man; operation (D106) 'be angry' — an inward flaring; target (D107) the righteous, at whose good the wicked burns. The coupling (D112) is flagged 'internal:ib-state' — the anger is coupled to the wicked's own interior condition, an inward reaction. The discovery (D114) reads v10: he sees the God-fearer's good fortune and is angry — envy turned to rage. So the movement here is perception (seeing the righteous blessed) leading to inward anger leading to outward manifestation. That outward manifestation surfaces in the locus row (D116), which reads 'paired with gnashing and melting': the anger is bound to its bodily expression — gnashing the teeth — and its self-consuming end — melting away, 'the desire of the wicked will perish.' Role (D115) characteristic. The silences: no source row (D103 present:false), though the narrative supplies the trigger (seeing the righteous prosper); no seat (D104=none) — not organ-lodged, though the gnashing and melting are bodily; no manner (D108=none); no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent), no separate effect (D111 absent) though the self-destructive outcome appears in the locus flag; no prohibition (D113 absent). In the inner-being frame the righteous is the occasion in the arena, but the reading holds on the wicked's interior: envy curdling into rage at another's blessing, a fury that turns on itself and dissolves. Read without valence bias, this is the family's descent-pole — anger as self-consuming resentment, ending in the melting-away of the one who harbours it.
narratives.story: At the very end of this psalm about the blessed, godly person, we glimpse the wicked man watching — and he is furious. Seeing the good that comes to the one who fears God, his envy curdles into rage. His anger shows itself in his body: he grinds his teeth. But then it turns on him and undoes him — he 'melts away', and everything he wanted comes to nothing. The poem does not spell out where the anger sits or how hot it burns; it shows the sequence: he sees, he seethes, he gnashes, he dissolves. It is resentment at someone else's blessing that ends up destroying the resenter.

narratives.narrative: achaz — to seize, grasp — is typed as a state (D102 type=state): the psalmist is passively gripped. Sense (D101) seize. Bearer (D105) the psalmist; operation (D106) 'be seized with indignation' — note the passive: the emotion takes hold of him rather than being wielded. Target (D107=none): the indignation has no object it strikes — it is a condition that overtakes, 'because of the wicked' as occasion but not as a victim it moves against; the silence marks this as a felt seizure, not aggression. Coupling (D112) is inferred as paired within its char-arc across the psalm — the indignation belongs to the sweep of the psalmist's devotion, one note in a larger movement. The discovery (D114) reads v53: hot indignation seizes him because of the wicked who forsake God's law — zeal-indignation, anger on behalf of the law. Locus (D116) internal:ib-state; role (D115) characteristic. This is the family's righteous-indignation pole, close kin to the psalm's zeal. The silences: no source (D103 present:false) — though the occasion (the wicked forsaking the law) is given, the row does not tag an inner spring; no seat (D104=none) — not organ-lodged despite the 'seizing'; no manner (D108=none); no intensity (D109 absent) — striking, given 'hot', yet no degree is flagged; no specifier (D110 absent), no effect (D111 absent) — where the seizure leads is not traced; no prohibition (D113 absent). In the inner-being frame the wicked are the occasion in the arena, but the reading rests on the psalmist's interior: a burning zeal that seizes him — anger not launched at a target but suffered as a grip, on behalf of God's forsaken law.
narratives.story: In this long psalm of love for God's law, the poet is suddenly gripped by a hot anger — indignation that seizes him when he sees wicked people abandoning what God has commanded. Notice how it comes: it takes hold of him, rather than being something he aims at anyone. There is no one he lashes out against; the feeling simply overwhelms him because of the disregard for the law he loves. It is one strong note within the whole song of his devotion. The poem does not say where the feeling sits, or measure how fierce it is, even though it calls it hot; it shows a person caught up in zeal, burning on God's behalf.

narratives.narrative: aph returns (its second reading), now typed as a state (D102 type=state) whose motion is active. Sense (D101) anger. Bearer (D105) the enemies; operation (D106) 'have anger ignite' — an event of kindling, fury flaring up; target (D107) 'to devour the people' — the anger reaches toward swallowing its victim alive. The coupling (D112) is flagged 'internal:ib-state' — the igniting anger coupled to the enemies' inner condition. The discovery (D114) reads v3: when their anger was kindled against us — hostile fury igniting, wrath flaring to the point of swallowing its victim alive. The locus row (D116) carries 'paired with the swallowing alive' — the anger bound to its devouring outcome, the near-catastrophe from which only the LORD's being 'on our side' delivered (v1-2). Role (D115) characteristic. The silences: no source (D103 present:false) — what kindled it is unstated; no seat (D104=none); no manner (D108=none); no intensity (D109 absent) — though 'kindled' and 'swallow alive' imply great heat, no degree is flagged; no specifier (D110 absent), no separate effect (D111 absent) though the devouring appears in the locus flag; no prohibition (D113 absent). In the inner-being frame the people are the object in the arena, but the reading holds on the enemies' interior: anger igniting into a devouring blaze.
narratives.story: This short song looks back on a narrow escape: if God had not been on their side, the poet says, their enemies' anger — once it flared up — would have swallowed them alive. Here the anger is caught in the moment of catching fire, blazing up to devour them like a flood. Unlike the settled grudge pictured elsewhere, this is anger igniting, reaching hungrily for its victim. The poem does not say what lit it, or where it sits, or how hot it grew; it ties the flaring fury straight to the near-disaster it almost caused. What saved them was not that the anger cooled, but that God stood with them against it.
narratives.variation_note: The second of two aph readings. At Psa 55:3 aph is a status with operation:none — anger frozen into a nursed grudge against the psalmist; here at Psa 124:3 aph is a state whose operation is 'have anger ignite', a kindling fury reaching to swallow its victim alive. The difference is settled-vs-igniting and static-vs-devouring: there anger has cooled into a borne resentment; here it flares as an active blaze. The same word thus spans both temperatures — smouldering grudge and sudden, consuming fire — and that range is itself the finding about how aph operates.

narratives.narrative: aph is here glossed 'wrath' and typed as a state (D102 type=state). Sense (D101) wrath. Bearer (D105) the enemies; operation (D106) 'be wrathful' — a condition of hostility they are in; target (D107) against the psalmist. The coupling (D112) is flagged 'internal:ib-state' — the wrath coupled to the enemies' inner condition. The discovery (D114) reads v7: against the wrath of the enemies, over which God stretches out his hand to deliver. The locus row (D116) carries 'paired with God's delivering hand' — the enemies' wrath bound not to a triumph but to its being overreached: God's hand stretches out against it. So the movement is: enemies in a wrathful state, aimed at the psalmist, met and countered by God's deliverance. Role (D115) characteristic. The silences: no source (D103 present:false) — the wrath's origin unstated; no seat (D104=none); no manner (D108=none); no intensity (D109 absent), no specifier (D110 absent), no separate effect (D111 absent) though the countering appears in the locus flag; no prohibition (D113 absent). In the inner-being frame the psalmist is the object and God the deliverer in the arena, but the reading holds on the enemies' interior: a wrathful hostility that, though real and aimed, is overmatched by the delivering hand stretched against it. Read without valence bias, this is the family's hostile-wrath pole set against the backdrop of rescue — the dark heat named precisely as the thing God's hand opposes.
narratives.story: Walking through trouble, the poet is surrounded by the fury of his enemies — but he is confident, because God reaches out his hand against that fury to save him. The enemies are in a state of wrath, aimed squarely at him, yet the poem frames it as something God overpowers rather than something that wins. It does not explain what stirred their anger, or where it sits, or how strong it is; it simply names their hostility and sets God's rescuing hand against it. The enemies' rage is real and pointed, but it is the very thing God stretches out to overcome.
